# Process discipline — bugs, completion, and issue hygiene

Workflow rules that operationalise Cardinal Rules 1 (correctness) and 4 (GitHub
issues are the plan and the log). Founding cases: [the evidence page](../../docs/development/evidence/process-discipline.md).

## Fix bugs immediately — never accumulate, never bury

When a bug is identified (a test failure, a review finding, a downstream
cascade, an L0 audit), the next code-touching action is the fix, before any new
feature work. A known bug downstream makes "new bug" indistinguishable from "old
bug propagated"; two bugs can partially cancel, so fixing one surfaces the
other; every test below a known bug has reduced evidential value; a refactor
over a buggy base carries the bug into the new abstraction (`[R]` user, the
Phase 3B debrief).

- check: bug known with the fix in progress on the same branch is acceptable;
  bug known with feature work proceeding in parallel is not. A large fix
  deferred by the user's explicit choice is deliberate; otherwise fix now, and
  when unsure stop the feature work, ask, fix, resume. It is never too late.
- tell: a commit adding a capability on top of an open red.

## Bias toward completion — finish known work while you hold the context

Do not defer work you know you will have to do to a future issue when this
session holds the context. Deferral is for a genuine cross-session or
cross-device handoff, never for punting finishable work.

- "No current consumer" often means "consumer not yet wired", not
  "speculative". check: before concluding a type or feature is unused, hunt for
  LATENT consumers, quantities the code already computes but has not typed or
  routed. [case](../../docs/development/evidence/process-discipline.md#2026-06-01-latent-consumer)
- check: separate the cheap, low-risk part (mint the type, do the rename: now)
  from the correctness-critical carve (wire it in: gated by test-architect and
  elegance review, still in-session if context allows).
- tell: an issue filed for a step whose every input is already in the session.

## Trust git for merge status — never a frozen memory claim

A memory or plan note saying a campaign is "not pushed / in-flight / on branch
X / not merged" is a point-in-time snapshot, written mid-flight when it was
true; the work merges in a later session and the note is never updated, so the
snapshot lies forward.

- check: before resuming, citing or acting on any "unmerged" claim,
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <hash> HEAD`; ancestor means merged means done,
  not active. Never trust the frozen claim over git.
  [case](../../docs/development/evidence/process-discipline.md#2026-06-21-seven-campaigns-in-flight)
- check, when resuming a plan: read the implementing class's first line before
  designing to a phase's prose (a scope read from prose is refuted by the
  realization), and re-check every "blocked by / not possible" claim, since a
  later phase of the same campaign may have dissolved the blocker.
- check, at merge time: a campaign note's terminal state is "merged @
  `<hash>`", the way a `Closes #NN` trailer closes an issue. After that it is
  archaeology: its lesson goes to an evidence page under
  `docs/development/evidence/`, its architectural milestone to the theory page's development history, and the note retires.
- A plan's internal task numbers COLLIDE with real GitHub issue numbers. check:
  never resolve "which issue tracks this?" from a plan's bare `#N`; read each
  candidate's title (`gh issue view N`), and the same before citing an issue in
  code, docs or a commit trailer. tell: a docs pass that redirects a retired
  claim to "#183 tracks this" is minting a new claim, and a closed or
  mis-numbered issue is the defect class the pass was removing.
- tell: a "resumed" campaign whose hash is already an ancestor; a clean tree
  that reads as unfinished.

## The two git prohibitions are enforced by a hook; the riders are not

`.claude/hooks/git-guard.py` (a PreToolUse hook on Bash) refuses `git add
-A|--all|.` and any `git commit` while HEAD is `main`, printing the reason. The
reason for the first: `scratch/` is a large, deliberately untracked working
directory (probes, memos, gate logs; `.gitignore` covers two of its
subdirectories), so the sweep is silent, and it lands inside a commit whose
subject describes something else, which is what lets it survive review.
[case](../../docs/development/evidence/process-discipline.md#2026-08-27-the-212-file-sweep)

- check: stage by path (`git add <paths>`), or `git add -u` when the change is
  confined to tracked files; before every commit read `git status --porcelain`
  (not `-uno`). The hook cannot read the staged set for you.
- Un-tracking a file by REWRITING history deletes it from the working tree:
  `filter-branch`/`filter-repo` finish by checking out the rewritten HEAD, and
  a file absent from the new tree is removed from disk, so the fix for an
  accidental commit destroys the working files the accident preserved. check:
  `cp -a` the directory aside BEFORE the rewrite, `diff -rq` after, restore
  with `cp -Rn`. Same family as the `git checkout` clause below: any git
  operation that writes the working tree is irrecoverable for untracked state.
- check, before pushing a rewrite: it is content-exact,
  `git diff --quiet <old-tip> <new-tip> -- . ':(exclude)<removed-paths>'`;
  empty means an already-run test gate carries over without a re-run.
- check, after a rewrite: every hash in the rewritten range changed, so plans,
  memories and issue comments citing one dangle (`plan-authoring` §7.1); grep
  the tracked corpus for the old short hashes, re-point them, and leave a
  banner saying a dangling hash in that range is re-found by commit SUBJECT.
- tell: a commit whose file list nobody re-read because they had just written
  its subject.

## A commit message with backticks is written with `-F`, never `-m`

zsh command-substitutes the backticks inside a double-quoted `-m "…"` argument,
so `` `x` `` becomes the output of running `x`, usually nothing, and the words
vanish from a permanent artefact with no diagnostic. This project's prose puts
backticks in nearly every commit message, so the exposure is every commit.

- check: write the message to a file, or `git commit -F -` from a QUOTED
  heredoc (`<<'MSG'`), then read it back with `git log -1 --format=%B` before
  pushing.
- tell: a subject line missing the word that was a code span
  ([L61](../../docs/development/evidence/lessons.md#l61-unvalidated-filter-clean), mechanism (b)).

## Mutation-testing an uncommitted file — never `git checkout` to revert

To prove a gate's teeth you mutate production code, run the gate (expect red),
then revert. If the file has uncommitted edits, `git checkout -- <file>`,
`git restore` and `git stash` revert to HEAD, destroying the uncommitted work,
not to the pre-mutation state
([L28](../../docs/development/evidence/lessons.md#l28-git-checkout-destroys)).

- check: revert a mutation by monkeypatching in-process, or copy the file to a
  tmp path and mutate the copy; reserve `git checkout`/`restore` for files you
  have NOT touched.
- The restore must be CRASH-safe, not merely exception-safe. A `try/finally`
  survives a failing test and not the thing that happens: the harness kills the
  battery (the 2-minute Bash timeout, a `pkill`, an interrupt), the `finally`
  never runs, and the file is left mutated on disk in a tree the next command
  commits. check: copy the pristine file aside BEFORE the first mutation and
  `diff -q` against the copy after the run; scope the battery to the files that
  can redden (N mutations times a full-suite run overruns the timeout by
  construction); check the file's integrity FIRST after any battery that did
  not print its own completion line.
  [case](../../docs/development/evidence/process-discipline.md#2026-08-18-the-battery-the-timeout-killed)
- tell: a `finally` offered as the restore.

## After pushing, look at CI — and baseline a red one before adding to it

"`main` is always green" is a claim about CI, true only if someone reads CI. A
CI that is ALREADY red cannot tell your regression from the inherited one:
`failure` before your push and `failure` after are identical output, zero
information (X1: a reading that cannot change carries nothing).

- check: on finding a red CI, establish the baseline before fixing or adding
  anything: read the last run from before your work and count what failed.
  Your contribution is then a subtraction, and both halves are reportable.
  [case](../../docs/development/evidence/process-discipline.md#2026-08-18-twenty-nine-of-thirty-red)
- tell: "it was already failing", true and exculpatory right up until it is
  your code.

## A refuted candidate is first-class output — record the structural reason

When an investigation rejects a hypothesis, frame, design or root-cause
candidate, the deliverable lists the rejected candidates with the one-line
structural reason each failed, never a bare "considered and rejected". The
reason is what stops the next session re-attacking a dead candidate; a
rejection without it is re-derived from scratch, at more than the original
cost, because the second attacker has less context on why it looked promising.

- check: qa (findings excluded from a report), numerics-investigator
  (hypotheses eliminated in the probe cascade), explorer (paths that
  dead-ended), cross-domain-attacker (the UNEXPLORED block) and the main agent
  in any plan that narrows a design space each owe the list.
- tell: "rejected" with no mechanism beside it.

## Don't file issues for what you'll fix this session

Issues are the cross-session handoff (Cardinal Rule 4). A finding that will be
remediated this session is fixed inline, not filed; a back-to-back open/close
is noise.

- check: after a review batch, split findings into inline-fixable-now (fix
  them) and cross-session follow-ups (file with `module:`/`level:`/`type:`
  labels). Sub-agents (qa, numerics-investigator) default to "file an issue for
  tracking": override that when in-session remediation is the plan.
- tell: an issue opened and closed in one session.
